title: The monk who was stoned
hookLine: Angulimala, now a monk, is hit with stones in town; told to bear it; his blessing eases a woman's birth (MN 86)

lines: A MONK IN THE SAME TOWNS.
cards: Changing is one thing. Getting everyone else to believe you've changed is another. The old reputation walks into every room before you do.
Angulimala is a monk now: head shaved, robe on, bowl in hand. Every morning he walks into town for alms, into the same towns whose people he terrorized. Mothers who lost sons.
Men who lost brothers. Today's story has two scenes in that town. In one, he brings a blessing.
In the other, he comes back bleeding.

teach.h: A WOMAN IN A HARD LABOR.
teach.b: The first scene. On his alms round, Angulimala passes a house where a woman is in a long, dangerous labor. He's shaken: how beings suffer.

He goes to the Buddha, who tells him to go back and say: sister, since I was born, I don't recall ever intending to take a life. By this truth, may you and your child be well. That would be a lie, Angulimala says.
I've killed many. So the Buddha changes one word.

teach.h: SINCE I WAS BORN WITH THE NOBLE BIRTH.
teach.b: Say instead: since I was born with the noble birth. Meaning, since I became a monk. He goes back and says it, and the woman and the baby are well.

In Theravada countries, monks still chant Angulimala's verse of truth for women near childbirth, and people keep it on paper and in homes. A man who took lives is remembered for helping bring them into the world.
The second scene. Another day in town, someone throws a clod of earth. Someone else, a stick.
Someone else, a shard of pottery.

teach.h: A HEAD BLEEDING, A BOWL BROKEN.
teach.b: He comes back with his head bleeding, his bowl broken, his robe torn.

teach.h: LIKE THE MOON FROM BEHIND A CLOUD.
teach.b: And the Buddha says, in effect: bear it. What you feel now is the result of what you did, and you're meeting it here, in this life. It's a hard word, and the sutta doesn't soften it.
There's no speech about how the townspeople should forgive him. Their anger is allowed to be real.
The old life has consequences, and the new life is real. Both at once. The sutta ends with Angulimala's own verses.
One compares a person who was careless and becomes careful to the moon coming out from behind a cloud, lighting up the world.

how: In Theravada countries such as Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar, monks chant the Angulimala Paritta, his verse of truth, as a blessing for women who are pregnant or in labor.

tell the Buddha it would be a lie.
games.why: he says it would be a lie. the Buddha changes one phrase: since I was born with the noble birth. true, and still a blessing.

practice: Think of someone in labor of any kind, straining to bring something into being: a friend expecting a baby, someone starting a business, finishing a degree, getting sober, trying to change.
Picture them in the middle of it, where it's hardest. Breathe out slowly, and wish them simply: may you be well, and may what you're bringing into the world be well.

wordCard.voice: Jati. Birth: the word Angulimala used for his new life as a monk, when he blessed a woman in labor.

orig.note: Pali: birth. Angulimala speaks of the 'noble birth' (ariya jati), his life as a monk.

carryVoice: Your line: born into a new life. The stones were real, and so was the blessing. That's day seventy-three.
